text: Source-available means source code is distributed along with the software, but does not necessarily grant OSI-style redistribution or commercial-use rights.
Licenses with a non-commercial use restriction are explicitly NOT OSI-approved open source licenses because they violate Open Source Definition clause 1 (Free Redistribution).
PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 grants all rights (copyright, patent, distribution, modification, change/new-work creation) for any noncommercial purpose.

text: Under PolyForm Noncommercial, a permitted purpose is any noncommercial purpose; the license expressly lists personal study, hobby, research, and use by charities/educational/research/public-safety/health/environmental/government organizations as permitted regardless of funding source.
PolyForm Noncommercial preserves all five freedoms typically associated with FOSS — use, study, modification, redistribution, and creation of derivative works — for noncommercial purposes.
PolyForm Noncommercial includes an attribution clause requiring the license terms and Required Notice lines travel with copies of the software.

PolyForm Strict 1.0.0 layers an additional Competing Use restriction on top of the noncommercial structure: even noncommercial use is forbidden if it competes with the licensor's products or services.
BUSL 1.1 permits non-production use (development, testing, evaluation) freely; production use is forbidden unless an Additional Use Grant is specified by the Licensor.
BUSL 1.1 automatically converts to a Change License (typically an OSI-approved license) on the Change Date or 4 years after first public distribution, whichever comes first.
BUSL 1.1 explicitly states: this License is not an Open Source license. Production use requires purchase of a commercial license.
BUSL 1.1 has been adopted by HashiCorp (Terraform, Vault, etc., August 2023), MariaDB, Couchbase, and others.

SSPL v1 Section 13 requires anyone offering the software (or a modified version) as a service to third parties to publish the Service Source Code of the entire service — including management, UI, API, automation, monitoring, backup, storage, and hosting software — under SSPL.
OSI, Debian, and Red Hat have all formally rejected SSPL as non-open-source, citing discriminatory field-of-use restrictions.

SSPL's Section 13 is widely considered too aggressive because it requires disclosure of unrelated infrastructure components, making it effectively impossible for SaaS companies to comply without becoming an SSPL shop.
Elastic License 2.0 prohibits providing the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service where the service provides users with access to any substantial set of features or functionality.
Elastic NV re-licensed from Apache 2.0 to Elastic License v2 in January 2021 in direct response to AWS offering Elasticsearch as a managed service without contributing back.
The Functional Source License (FSL) is a Fair Source license that converts to Apache 2.0 or MIT after two years, designed for SaaS companies that value both user freedom and developer sustainability.

FSL grants rights for non-production use freely (study, research, evaluation) and for production use only if the use does not compete with the licensor by offering the Software as a hosted or managed service.
FSL was originally created by Sentry and is used by other SaaS companies seeking delayed-open-source terms.

PolyForm Strict is the variant of PolyForm Noncommercial specifically designed to block the SaaS-style resale case where a third party offers the software as a hosted or managed service in competition with the licensor.
Each of these source-available licenses has a stable SPDX identifier: PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0, PolyForm-Strict-1.0.0, BUSL-1.1, SSPL-1.0, Elastic-2.0, FSL-1.1-MIT, FSL-1.1-Apache.

U.S. copyright law (17 U.S.C. § 106) grants copyright owners exclusive rights to reproduce, prepare derivative works, distribute, perform, and display. Software licenses operate as contracts reserving some of these rights while granting others.
Heather Meeker is the principal attorney who drafted the PolyForm Project licenses, BUSL 1.1, SSPL v1, and the Elastic License, and is the most-cited authority on source-available licensing.

PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 best matches the user's stated requirement (maximum user freedom, no user monetization) because it grants the broadest set of rights subject only to a noncommercial-purpose restriction, with a clean noncommercial purpose definition that explicitly preserves internal business use, charity/educational/research use, and personal use.

PolyForm Strict 1.0.0 is the runner-up when SaaS-style competing resale is also a concern; Elastic License v2 and FSL are narrower alternatives focused on the SaaS/managed-service carve-out specifically.

BUSL 1.1 and SSPL v1 are NOT ideal for the stated requirement because BUSL 1.1's four-year time-delayed conversion leaves an initial period of restrictive terms, and SSPL's Section 13 requires disclosure of unrelated service infrastructure (effectively incompatible with normal SaaS operations).
BUSL's ambiguity led to the OpenTofu fork of Terraform — community signal that BUSL's restrictions, while enforceable, generate developer friction when adoption is broad.

Parity Public License 7.0.0 is source-available with copyleft-style requirements: derivative works must be shared under the same terms; not a pure noncommercial license but a source-available share-alike.

Hippocratic License 3.0 is an MIT-style license with added ethical-use restrictions (no harm to human rights). It restricts use on ethical grounds rather than monetization grounds — adjacent but different from a no-monetization license.
PolyForm Internal Use restricts use of the software to within the licensed organization — it prohibits distribution but does not by itself prohibit monetization through internal use.
PolyForm Free Trial permits evaluation only for up to 32 consecutive calendar days.
